question: What is the main focus of microbiology in nursing?

options.A: Studying organisms too small to see without magnification
options.B: Examining macroscopic parasites found in stagnant water
options.C: Analyzing chemical imbalances in human blood samples
options.D: Measuring the physical growth rate of pediatric patients

explanation: Microbiology is all about tiny living things like bacteria and viruses that we need a microscope to see. Super straightforward! [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to understand how microbes behave?

options.A: To diagnose complex genetic disorders without laboratory tests
options.B: To manufacture prescription antibiotics in hospital pharmacies
options.C: To anticipate and prevent infections in vulnerable patients
options.D: To eliminate all bacteria living on human skin permanently

explanation: When you know how germs live and spread, you can protect your patients better. You've got this! [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h1)

question: What do we call the natural home where a germ lives and multiplies?
explanation: Think of a reservoir as the germ's cozy home—like soil, water, or a human body—where it hangs out and multiplies. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h2)

question: An insect bite that transfers a malaria parasite to a human is an example of which link in the chain of infection?
explanation: Vectors like mosquitoes are just the transport system moving the germ from one place to another! [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the single most effective way to stop the spread of hospital infections?
explanation: Good old handwashing is your superpower in the ward. It physically removes germs before they can cause trouble. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h3)

question: When do you strictly need surgical asepsis (complete sterility) during routine nursing tasks?

options.A: When assisting an ambulatory patient to walk in the hallway
options.B: While taking a patient's temperature with an oral thermometer
options.C: During the insertion of an indwelling urinary catheter
options.D: During the physical assessment of a patient with a cough

explanation: Since the bladder is normally sterile, sliding a catheter in means everything must be 100% germ-free to prevent UTIs. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h3)

question: What causes germs to become resistant to antibiotics?

options.A: Overuse and misuse of prescribed drugs

explanation: Using antibiotics wrongly or stopping them too early gives germs a chance to figure out how to fight back and survive. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h4)

question: A patient stops taking their antibiotics early because they feel better. What is the big risk here?

options.A: Survival of resistant microbes that multiply and worsen the illness
options.B: Immediate elimination of all remaining bacteria in the body
options.C: Permanent immunity to all future respiratory infections
options.D: Rapid enhancement of the body's natural white blood cell count

explanation: Stopping early kills the weak germs, leaving behind the toughest ones to bounce back stronger. Always finish the dose! [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h4)

question: When is the best time to collect a wound culture swab?

options.B: While the patient is receiving topical antiseptics
options.C: Immediately after finishing the antibiotic course
options.D: Twenty-four hours after a dressing change

explanation: Always grab your culture before giving antibiotics, otherwise the drugs might kill the germs in your sample and give you a false negative! [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h5)

question: What happens if a clinical lab specimen gets contaminated with normal skin germs?

options.A: Misleading laboratory results leading to improper treatment
options.B: Automatic clearance of the sample by the hospital pharmacy
options.C: Instant destruction of the laboratory testing equipment
options.D: Immediate resolution of the patient's underlying infection

explanation: Skin germs can sneak into your sample and trick the lab into treating the wrong thing. Good technique keeps samples clean! [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h5)

question: How do standard vaccines help build active immunity in the body?

options.A: By destroying all white blood cells to reset the immune system
options.B: By introducing weakened or killed antigens to trigger antibody production
options.C: By supplying readymade antibodies directly from an animal source
options.D: By coating the digestive tract with chemical barriers against viruses

explanation: Vaccines give your immune system a safe practice run so it knows how to fight the real germ later. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is the main community benefit of achieving high rates of herd immunity?

options.A: Protecting vulnerable individuals who cannot receive vaccines safely
options.B: Preventing all forms of chronic non-communicable diseases permanently
options.C: Eliminating the need for basic handwashing and environmental sanitation
options.D: Ensuring that viral pathogens mutate into completely harmless plants

explanation: When most people are vaccinated, it creates a shield around babies and sick people who can't take vaccines themselves. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which sign is a classic clue that a wound has a localized infection?

options.A: Cool skin temperature around the site
options.B: Rapid reduction in local pain levels
options.C: Pale and dry wound bed surfaces

explanation: Pus and a bad smell mean white blood cells are hard at work fighting off an active bacterial invasion. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h7)

question: Why do clinicians prefer targeted antibiotics over broad-spectrum drugs when treating wound infections?

options.A: It minimizes resistance and effectively targets the specific cultured pathogen
options.B: It prevents the patient from experiencing any drug side effects
options.C: It eliminates all normal skin bacteria across the entire body
options.D: It guarantees that the wound will close within twenty-four hours

explanation: Using the exact right drug for the specific germ stops us from creating superbugs with unnecessary broad-spectrum meds. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h7)
